Let $G$ be a finite abelian group with character dual $\widehat G$ ([[def-qa-finite-abelian-character-dual]]). For a subgroup $H\le G$ ([[def-subgroup]]), define its character annihilator by
$$H^{\perp}:=\{\chi\in\widehat G:\chi(h)=1\text{ for every }h\in H\}.$$
For any subset $K\subseteq\widehat G$ (in particular, for any subgroup once $\widehat G$ has been proved to be a group), define
$$K^{\perp}:=\{g\in G:\chi(g)=1\text{ for every }\chi\in K\}.$$
The pairing is evaluation, and the same convention is used in both directions. `lem-qa-finite-abelian-annihilators-are-subgroups` proves that these sets are subgroups when the input is a subgroup.

Let $G$ be a finite abelian group and $H\le G$. Under the canonical evaluation identification $G\cong\widehat{\widehat G}$,
$$(H^\perp)^\perp=H.$$
For a finite abelian group $G$, the pointwise product, constant-one identity and pointwise inverse on $\widehat G$ make it a finite abelian group. Its order is $|\widehat G|=|G|$.

Let $G$ be a finite abelian group ([[def-group]]), written **additively**: its
operation is written $+$, its identity is written $0$, and its underlying set is
finite. Let $\mathbb C^{\times}$ be the group of units of the field $\mathbb C$
([[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]], [[lem-ring-units-form-a-group]]), that
is, the nonzero complex numbers under multiplication.

An **additive character** of $G$ is a group homomorphism
([[def-group-homomorphism]])

$$\chi:G\longrightarrow\mathbb C^{\times},\qquad \chi(x+y)=\chi(x)\,\chi(y)\quad(x,y\in G).$$

Write $\widehat G$ for the set of all additive characters of $G$. Since $G$ and
$\mathbb C^{\times}$ are groups, every additive character automatically
satisfies $\chi(0)=1$ and $\chi(-x)=\chi(x)^{-1}$
([[lem-group-homomorphism-basic-properties]]), so multiplicativity is the whole
requirement.

**This is not the representation-theoretic character.** The word "character"
already names the function $\chi_V(g)=\operatorname{tr}(\rho_V(g))$ attached to
a finite-dimensional complex representation $V$ of $G$
([[def-character-of-a-complex-representation]],
[[def-finite-dimensional-representation-of-a-group-over-a-field]]). That
function need not be multiplicative — only for a one-dimensional representation
is it a homomorphism to $\mathbb C^{\times}$ — and the next item proves the
precise bridge: the additive characters of a finite abelian group are exactly
the characters of its one-dimensional complex representations, and exactly its
irreducible ones.

**Well-definedness.** $\widehat G$ is defined as a set of functions
$G\to\mathbb C^{\times}$, so the definition itself selects nothing. In
particular it chooses no decomposition of $G$, no enumeration of $G$, and no
isomorphism $G\cong\widehat G$, and it asserts nothing here about a group
structure on $\widehat G$; the dictionary proved in the next item records what
structure there is.

Let $G$ be a group ([[def-group]]) with identity $e$. A subset $H \subseteq G$ is
a **subgroup** of $G$, written $H \le G$, when

- **(S1)** $e \in H$;
- **(S2)** $H$ is closed under the operation: $x, y \in H$ implies $xy \in H$
  ([[def-binary-operation]]);
- **(S3)** $H$ is closed under inverses: $x \in H$ implies $x^{-1} \in H$.

By (S2) the operation of $G$ restricts to a binary operation on $H$; it is
associative there because it is associative on $G$, the element $e$ of (S1) is a
two-sided identity for it ([[def-identity-element]]), and (S3) supplies for each
$x \in H$ a two-sided inverse lying in $H$ ([[def-invertible-element]]). So a
subgroup, with the restricted operation, is itself a group, and its identity and
its inverses are those of $G$.

Every group $G$ has the two **trivial subgroups** $\{e\}$ and $G$ itself; a
subgroup $H$ with $H \ne G$ is called **proper**.

For a finite abelian group $G$, give $\widehat G$ its pointwise multiplication. Its dual $\widehat{\widehat G}$ consists of functions $\Phi:\widehat G\to\mathbb C^{\times}$ satisfying $\Phi(\chi\psi)=\Phi(\chi)\Phi(\psi)$. The evaluation map
$$\operatorname{ev}:G\longrightarrow\widehat{\widehat G},\qquad \operatorname{ev}(g)(\chi):=\chi(g),$$
is a group isomorphism. The map itself is canonical; a decomposition into cyclic factors is used only to prove it is injective.
Let $G$ be a finite abelian group. For every subgroup $H\le G$, $H^\perp$ is a subgroup of $\widehat G$. For every subgroup $K\le\widehat G$, $K^\perp$ is a subgroup of $G$.

derivations.claim: Choose $g\in K\setminus H$. Under the canonical evaluation identification [F5], [F1] gives $(H^\perp)^\perp=H$, so there is $\chi_0\in H^\perp$ with $\chi_0(g)\ne1$. By [F6], $H^\perp$ is a group; the evaluation map $\epsilon_g:H^\perp\to\mathbb C^\times$, $\epsilon_g(\chi)=\chi(g)$, is a homomorphism because pointwise multiplication gives $\epsilon_g(\chi\psi)=\chi(g)\psi(g)$. Its image is finite by [F2] and is a subgroup because it is the image of a group homomorphism. It contains $1$ and the nonidentity value $\chi_0(g)$, so it has at least two elements.

Every nonempty fiber of $\epsilon_g$ is a coset of its kernel: $\epsilon_g(\chi)=\epsilon_g(\psi)$ exactly when $\epsilon_g(\chi\psi^{-1})=1$. Therefore at most half of $H^\perp$ maps to $1$. A uniform $\chi\in H^\perp$ has $\chi(g)\ne1$ with probability at least $1/2$, and each such character is nontrivial on $K$ because $g\in K$.

For any $\chi\in H^\perp$, every $h\in H$ satisfies $\chi(h)=1$, so $H\subseteq K\cap\ker\chi$. The set $\ker\chi$ is a subgroup: it contains $0$ by [F3], and the homomorphism law gives closure under addition and inverses. Its intersection with $K$ is a subgroup by [F4]. If $\chi|_K\ne1$, the homomorphism $\chi|_K$ has at least two values; its fibers are cosets of $K\cap\ker\chi$, so $[K:K\cap\ker\chi]=|\chi(K)|\ge2$.

Let $G$ be a finite abelian group, and let $H\subsetneq K\le G$. Choose a character $\chi$ uniformly from $H^\perp$. Then
$$\mathbb P(\chi|_K\ne 1)\ge \frac12.$$
For every outcome with $\chi|_K\ne1$, the updated common kernel $K\cap\ker\chi$, where $\ker\chi=\{g\in G:\chi(g)=1\}$, contains $H$ and has index at least two in $K$.

Let $X_1,\ldots,X_N$ be mutually independent Bernoulli$(p_i)$ variables on a finite probability space. Set $S=\sum_iX_i$ and $\mu=\sum_i p_i$. For $\delta\ge0$,
$$\mathbb P(S\ge(1+\delta)\mu)\le\exp\{-\mu((1+\delta)\log(1+\delta)-\delta)\}.$$
For $0\le\delta<1$,
$$\mathbb P(S\le(1-\delta)\mu)\le\exp\{-\mu(\delta+(1-\delta)\log(1-\delta))\}.$$
For $0\le\delta\le1$ the upper and lower tails are respectively at most $\exp(-\mu\delta^2/3)$ and $\exp(-\mu\delta^2/2)$, and
$$\mathbb P(|S-\mu|\ge\delta\mu)\le2\exp(-\mu\delta^2/3).$$
At $\delta=1$ the lower optimized bound is $\exp(-\mu)$, proved directly rather than by taking $\log0$. Empty sums and $\mu=0$ are included. Also, for $N>0$ and $t\ge0$,
$$\mathbb P(|S-\mu|\ge t)\le2\exp(-2t^2/N).$$

derivations.claim: If $s$ cuts have occurred, repeated halving gives $|K|\le N/2^s\le1$. Since $H\le K$ and a subgroup contains the identity, this forces $K=H$. Consequently, on the event $K_M\ne H$, the process remained strictly above $H$ for all $M$ trials and fewer than $s$ actual cuts occurred.

Couple each trial, while $K_{t-1}>H$, by first drawing its cut indicator $C_t$ with conditional probability $p_t\ge1/2$ and then drawing $\chi_t$ from the uniform distribution conditioned on that indicator. If $C_t=1$, draw an auxiliary $Y_t\in\{0,1\}$ with conditional probability $\mathbb P(Y_t=1\mid C_t=1,\text{past})=1/(2p_t)$; if $C_t=0$, set $Y_t=0$. Then $Y_t\le C_t$ and $\mathbb P(Y_t=1\mid\text{past})=1/2$. After the process reaches $H$, draw fresh independent $Y_t\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(1/2)$. Thus the $Y_t$ are independent Bernoulli$(1/2)$ variables, and on every failure outcome $\sum_tY_t\le\sum_tC_t<s$.

Let $X:=\sum_{t=1}^M Y_t$ and $\mu=M/2$. The coupling and Step 1.1 give $\mathbb P(K_M\ne H)\le\mathbb P(X<s)$. Since $\mu\ge2s+8\ln(1/\delta)$, we have $s\le\mu/2$, so $\{X<s\}\subseteq\{X\le\mu/2\}$.

Apply [F2] with $\eta=1/2$ to obtain $\mathbb P(X\le\mu/2)\le e^{-\mu/8}$. The bound on $\mu$ implies $e^{-\mu/8}\le e^{-\ln(1/\delta)}=\delta$. Hence $\mathbb P(K_M\ne H)\le\delta$. If $H=K_0$, the process stays at $H$ by definition, giving the stated zero failure probability.

An input group is given in explicit invariant-factor coordinates
$$G=\prod_{i=1}^r\mathbb Z/n_i\mathbb Z,\qquad 2\le n_1\mid n_2\mid\cdots\mid n_r,$$
with componentwise addition and $N:=|G|=\prod_i n_i$. The empty product has $G=\{0\}$ and $N=1$. No procedure for finding these coordinates from a black-box group is included. A character label is a tuple $\mathbf k=(k_1,\ldots,k_r)$ with $k_i\in\mathbb Z/n_i\mathbb Z$, representing
$$\chi_{\mathbf k}(\mathbf g):=\prod_{i=1}^r\exp(2\pi i k_i g_i/n_i).$$
The cyclic-character and product-character suppliers identify these labels with all of $\widehat G$.

The hiding input is a finite set $S$, an injective encoding $\eta:S\to\{0,1\}^m$, and a total function $F:G\to S$ for which there is an unknown subgroup $H\le G$ such that
$$F(\mathbf g)=F(\mathbf g')\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \mathbf g-\mathbf g'\in H.$$
This is the hiding promise. Put $b_i:=\lceil\log_2 n_i\rceil$ and $b:=\sum_i b_i$. Encode $g_i\in\mathbb Z/n_i\mathbb Z$ by the $b_i$-bit big-endian binary word of its least residue in $\{0,\ldots,n_i-1\}$, and encode $\mathbf g$ by concatenating these words in coordinate order; denote this injective code by $\operatorname{code}_G(\mathbf g)$. This uses the first-wire-most-significant-bit convention of [[def-qc-ordered-bitstring-encoding]]. Use the same coordinate widths and convention to encode character labels $\mathbf k$ as $\operatorname{code}_{\widehat G}(\mathbf k)$.

The hiding input also supplies a total Boolean function $\widetilde F:\{0,1\}^b\to\{0,1\}^m$ agreeing with $\eta\circ F$ on valid group codes; its values on invalid bit strings are part of the declared extension. The coherent XOR oracle acts by
$$O_{\widetilde F}|x,y\rangle=|x,y\oplus\widetilde F(x)\rangle$$
on all ordered input and target bit-string basis states. In particular, on valid codes it adds $\eta(F(\mathbf g))$ to the target. A named oracle call is charged as one query; a Boolean-circuit implementation is charged for its reversible gates. The model makes no claim that an arbitrary function has an efficient circuit.

$$K:=\{\mathbf g\in G:\chi_{\mathbf k^{(j)}}(\mathbf g)=1\text{ for every }1\le j\le M\}=\bigcap_{j=1}^M\ker\chi_{\mathbf k^{(j)}},$$
where $\ker\chi:=\{\mathbf g:\chi(\mathbf g)=1\}$ and the empty intersection is defined to be $G$. Success means $K=H$. The output remains this implicit common-kernel presentation; converting it to subgroup generators is outside the definition.

Let $n,m\ge0$ and let $f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}^m$ be a total Boolean function on ordered bit strings. Its coherent XOR oracle is the linear extension of
$$
O_f|x,y\rangle=|x,y\oplus f(x)\rangle
$$
on the ordered input and target computational basis, where XOR is componentwise. The declared access contract states how many invocations count as queries and whether a controlled invocation is supplied. A query to this declared black box is counted separately from elementary gate size, depth, and width.

If $f$ is supplied instead by an explicit Boolean circuit, implementing $O_f$ means compiling that circuit and paying its reversible elementary-gate and workspace costs; the function description alone is not a free query. For this XOR oracle, its inverse is the same map, as proved in [[thm-qc-reversible-xor-oracle-unitary]]. Controlled access remains a separate capability unless the contract explicitly provides it.

For a complex vector space $H$, write $\operatorname{End}(H)$ for the set of
linear maps $H\to H$ ([[def-linear-map]]).

Let $H_A,H_B$ be finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces with fixed
ordered orthonormal bases $(e_i)_{i<a}$ and $(f_j)_{j<b}$, respectively. The
ordered product basis of $H_A\otimes H_B$ has the $A$ index first. For
$R\in\operatorname{End}(H_A\otimes H_B)$ define
$\operatorname{Tr}_B(R)\in\operatorname{End}(H_A)$ by

$$\bigl(\operatorname{Tr}_B(R)\bigr)_{i i'}:=\sum_{j<b}R_{(i,j),(i',j)}.$$

Rows are output coordinates and columns are input coordinates, as in
[[def-coordinate-column-and-matrix-of-a-linear-map]]. If $b=0$, the sum is
empty and equals $0$. The notation $\operatorname{Tr}_B$ means that the second
factor is contracted; the first factor and its order are retained.

For an integer $d\ge 1$, the $d$-level register is the complex inner-product
space $Q_d=\mathbb C^d$ with the standard pairing
$\langle z,w\rangle_{\rm root}=\sum_{j<d}z_j\overline{w_j}$, linear in the
first argument as in [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]] and
[[prop-standard-coordinate-inner-products]]. Its **computational basis** is the
ordered standard basis $(e_0,\ldots,e_{d-1})$ of [[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]].
The register's alphabet is the ordered set $\{0,\ldots,d-1\}$.

For $n\ge0$, the $n$-qubit register is the ordered tensor product over
$\mathbb C$ of $n$ copies of $Q_2$. Here $\otimes_{\mathbb C}$ is the algebraic
module tensor product ([[def-tensor-product-of-modules-by-generators-and-relations]]),
with its complex-module structure and finite iterated/empty-product conventions
from [[thm-commutative-ring-module-structure-on-a-tensor-product]] and
[[cor-finite-iterated-tensor-products-represent-multilinear-maps]]. The tuple of
bit positions is ordered lexicographically, with the first wire as the most
significant position; the product-basis theorem below establishes the
corresponding elementary tensors as a basis. For $n=0$, the empty tensor
product is $\mathbb C$ with basis $\{1\}$. This one-dimensional trivial
register is distinct from the zero vector space $\mathbb C^0$. By definition a
register has positive dimension; a zero-dimensional space may still occur as a
factor in the more general tensor-space construction below.

For every $d\ge1$, the ordered computational basis $(e_0,\ldots,e_{d-1})$ of
the register $Q_d$ from [[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]] is an
orthonormal basis for its declared inner product. Separately, the one-dimensional
zero-qubit register has the basis $\{1\}$ by definition.

An **ordered tensor register** consists of a finite ordered list of
finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H_0,\ldots,H_{n-1}$, each
equipped with a specified ordered orthonormal basis. Its space is
$H_0\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{n-1}$, with factors retained in the displayed
order. The product basis is ordered lexicographically by its tuple of factor
indices. The empty tensor product is $\mathbb C$ with basis $\{1\}$. A
zero-dimensional factor is allowed in this mathematical construction and makes
the tensor space zero; it is not a register under
[[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]].

The inner product is linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the
second, and on elementary tensors it is

$$\left\langle\bigotimes_{k<n}x_k,\bigotimes_{k<n}y_k\right\rangle_{\otimes}:=\prod_{k<n}\langle x_k,y_k\rangle_{{\rm root},k}.$$ 

For the empty tensor, the right side is the empty product $1$, giving the
standard inner product on $\mathbb C$.

For a permutation $\sigma$ of the $n$ factor positions, the **wire permutation**
$P_\sigma$ maps the product basis vector indexed by
$(i_0,\ldots,i_{n-1})$ to the product basis vector whose output factor order is
$(\sigma(0),\ldots,\sigma(n-1))$. It is extended linearly; for $n=0$ it is the
identity on $\mathbb C$. The extension is a linear map in the sense of
[[def-linear-map]].

Let $H_0,\ldots,H_{n-1}$ be a finite ordered list of finite-dimensional
complex inner-product spaces with specified ordered orthonormal bases of
sizes $d_0,\ldots,d_{n-1}$, allowing $d_k=0$. The elementary tensors of the
factor bases, ordered lexicographically, form an orthonormal basis of the
tensor register, and

$$\dim(H_0\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{n-1})=\prod_{k<n}d_k.$$

For the empty list the product is $1$ and the tensor space is $\mathbb C$; if
any $d_k=0$, the tensor space is zero and the product basis is empty.

Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space, with the root library's convention that the inner product is linear in its first argument. A **density operator** on $H$ is a non-negative endomorphism $\rho:H\to H$ with $\operatorname{tr}(\rho)=1$; non-negative and trace have the meanings of [[def-non-negative-and-positive-operator]] and [[def-trace-of-an-endomorphism]]. The zero-dimensional space is excluded: its only endomorphism has trace $0$.

Here $\ker\rho=\{x\in H:\rho x=0\}$, using the kernel of a linear map from [[def-kernel-and-image-of-a-linear-map]]. The **support** of $\rho$ is the orthogonal complement of its kernel in the root convention:

$$\operatorname{supp}(\rho):=\{x\in H: \langle x,y\rangle=0\text{ for every }y\in\ker\rho\}.$$

For a subspace $S\subseteq H$, $\rho$ is **faithful on $S$** when $\operatorname{supp}(\rho)=S$ and the restriction $\rho|_S:S\to S$ is positive definite in the sense of [[def-non-negative-and-positive-operator]]. This restriction is an endomorphism: if $x\in S$ and $y\in\ker\rho$, self-adjointness gives $\langle\rho x,y\rangle=\langle x,\rho y\rangle=0$, so $\rho x\in(\ker\rho)^\perp=S$.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space and let
$T:V\to V$ be linear. The operator $T$ is **non-negative** when $T$ is
self-adjoint in the sense of [[def-self-adjoint-and-normal-endomorphism]] and

$$\langle Tv,v\rangle\ge 0$$

for every $v\in V$.

The operator $T$ is **positive** when $T$ is self-adjoint and

$$\langle Tv,v\rangle>0$$

for every nonzero $v\in V$.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional vector space over $F$ and let $T:V\to V$ be
linear. Choose any ordered basis $\mathcal B$ of $V$ and define the **trace of
the endomorphism $T$** by

$$\operatorname{tr}(T):=\operatorname{tr}([T]_{\mathcal B}^{\mathcal B}).$$

This is independent of the chosen basis: matrices of the same endomorphism in
two ordered bases are similar, and similar matrices have equal trace. When
$V$ is the zero space, the empty basis gives trace $0$.

For every natural $n$, the map
$\operatorname{tr}:M_n(F)\to F$ is linear:

$$\operatorname{tr}(A+B)=\operatorname{tr}(A)+\operatorname{tr}(B),\qquad \operatorname{tr}(\lambda A)=\lambda\operatorname{tr}(A).$$

All complex inner products in this track use the root convention: they are
linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second
([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]). For vectors $x,y$ in the same
space, define the Dirac pairing by

$$\langle x|y\rangle_D:=\langle y,x\rangle_{\mathrm{root}}.$$

The ket $|x\rangle$ denotes the vector $x$. The bra $\langle x|$ denotes the
linear functional $z\mapsto\langle z,x\rangle_{\mathrm{root}}$.

For finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H,K$, vectors $y\in H$ and
$x\in K$, define the rank-one linear map

$$|x\rangle\langle y|:H\to K,\qquad z\mapsto\langle z,y\rangle_{H,\mathrm{root}}x.$$

Given ordered orthonormal bases of $H$ and $K$, its coordinate matrix is
$[x][y]^\dagger$, where $[x]$ and $[y]$ are the corresponding coordinate
columns and $M^\dagger:=\overline M^{\mathsf T}$ is the conjugate transpose.
The coordinate assertion is established in
[[thm-qc-dirac-notation-coordinate-identity]].

derivations.claim: Write $N=|G|$ and $h=|H|$. The oracle output on the initial state is $|\Psi\rangle=N^{-1/2}\sum_{g\in G}|\operatorname{code}_G(g)\rangle|\eta(F(g))\rangle$. The unreduced density matrix has terms $N^{-1}|\operatorname{code}_G(g)\rangle\langle\operatorname{code}_G(g')|\otimes|\eta(F(g))\rangle\langle\eta(F(g'))|$. By [L1] and output-register orthonormality [F3], tracing out the second register retains exactly the pairs with $\eta(F(g))=\eta(F(g'))$. Injectivity of $\eta$ in [F2] makes this equivalent to $F(g)=F(g')$.

By [F1], the retained pairs are exactly those lying in a common coset $C\in G/H$. Translation gives $|C|=h$. By [F3], the vectors $|g\rangle$ are orthonormal, so $\langle C,C\rangle=h^{-1}\sum_{g,g'\in C}\langle g,g'\rangle=1$ for $|C\rangle:=h^{-1/2}\sum_{g\in C}|g\rangle$. Hence $\rho_G=N^{-1}\sum_{C\in G/H}\sum_{g,g'\in C}|g\rangle\langle g'|$. The rank-one matrix $|C\rangle\langle C|$ has diagonal entries $1/h$ on the $h$ labels in $C$ and zero elsewhere, so its trace is $1$ by [F5]. By [F6], $|C\rangle\langle C|v=\langle v,C\rangle_{\rm root}|C\rangle$, hence $\langle |C\rangle\langle C|v,v\rangle_{\rm root}=|\langle v,C\rangle_{\rm root}|^2\ge0$. Therefore $|C\rangle\langle C|=h^{-1}\sum_{g,g'\in C}|g\rangle\langle g'|$.

Substitution gives $\rho_G=(h/N)\sum_{C\in G/H}|C\rangle\langle C|$. Each summand is nonnegative by step 2.1, so $\rho_G$ is nonnegative. The cosets partition the $N$ group elements into blocks of size $h$, so there are $N/h$ distinct cosets and the weights sum to $(h/N)(N/h)=1$. By trace linearity [F5] and the unit trace of each summand, $\operatorname{tr}(\rho_G)=1$. Thus [F4] makes $\rho_G$ a density operator, and the formula is the uniform mixture over distinct cosets.

Let $G$ be finite abelian, $H\le G$, and $x_0\in G$. Put $N:=|G|$, $M:=|H|$, and $Q:=|H^\perp|$, which is finite by [[thm-qa-finite-abelian-subgroup-annihilator-cardinality]]. Write $N_{\mathbb R}:=\iota_{\mathbb R}(N)$, $M_{\mathbb R}:=\iota_{\mathbb R}(M)$, and $Q_{\mathbb R}:=\iota_{\mathbb R}(Q)$ for their canonical real images, as in [[def-qa-normalized-finite-abelian-fourier-transform]]. These are positive since $G$ and $H$ contain their identities and $H^\perp$ contains the trivial character, and they are viewed in $\mathbb C$ through its embedded copy of $\mathbb R$. For the indicator $1_{x_0+H}$,
$$F_G1_{x_0+H}(\chi)=\begin{cases}M_{\mathbb R}N_{\mathbb R}^{-1/2}\overline{\chi(x_0)},&\chi\in H^\perp,\\0,&\chi\notin H^\perp.\end{cases}$$
Consequently, the normalized uniform-coset function $M_{\mathbb R}^{-1/2}1_{x_0+H}$ transforms to the function supported on $H^\perp$ with value $M_{\mathbb R}^{1/2}N_{\mathbb R}^{-1/2}\overline{\chi(x_0)}=Q_{\mathbb R}^{-1/2}\overline{\chi(x_0)}$ there. The unnormalized indicator amplitude and normalized-state amplitude are distinct.
If $G$ is a finite abelian group, $\chi:G\to\mathbb C^{\times}$ is an additive character, and $x\in G$, then $|\chi(x)|=1$.

Let $G$ be finite abelian, $H\le G$, $N=|G|$, and $h=|H|$. Write $\mathcal C_H:=\{g+H:g\in G\}$ for the set of distinct additive cosets, where $g+H:=\{g+h':h'\in H\}$. Start with the uniform group state, evaluate an exact hiding oracle into a fresh output register, then discard that register. On the group register the resulting density matrix is
$$\rho_G=\frac{h}{N}\sum_{C\in\mathcal C_H}|C\rangle\langle C|,\qquad |C\rangle:=h^{-1/2}\sum_{g\in C}|g\rangle.$$
Thus it is the uniform mixture of one normalized coset state for each distinct coset.

For a subgroup $H\le G$ of a finite abelian group, restriction and inflation identify $H^\perp$ with the character dual of $G/H$. Consequently
$$|H^\perp|=|G/H|=[G:H]=\frac{|G|}{|H|},\qquad |H^\perp|\,|H|=|G|.$$
The quotient convention is left cosets, with additive notation.

Let $N_{\mathbb R}$ be the canonical positive real image of $|G|$ from [[def-qa-normalized-finite-abelian-fourier-transform]]. Define the finite coefficient matrix $U$, with rows indexed by $\widehat G$ and columns by $G$, by
$$U_{\chi,x}=N_{\mathbb R}^{-1/2}\overline{\chi(x)},\qquad \chi\in\widehat G,\ x\in G.$$
It is square and satisfies $U^*U=I_G$ and $UU^*=I_{\widehat G}$, where $U^*$ is the conjugate transpose and $I_X$ is the identity matrix indexed by $X$, with $(I_X)_{x,y}=1$ when $x=y$ and $0$ otherwise. These two identities are the meaning of “unitary” here.

For a finite abelian group $G$ and $x,y\in G$,
$$\sum_{\chi\in\widehat G}\chi(x)\overline{\chi(y)}=\begin{cases}|G|,&x=y,\\0,&x\ne y.\end{cases}$$
This is orthogonality of the columns indexed by group elements. It is proved from cyclic root sums and is not inferred from row orthogonality.

Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space, with the root library's convention that the inner product is linear in its first argument. A **density operator** on $H$ is a non-negative endomorphism $\rho:H\to H$ with $\operatorname{tr}(\rho)=1$; non-negative and trace have the meanings of [[def-non-negative-and-positive-operator]] and [[def-trace-of-an-endomorphism]]. The zero-dimensional space is excluded: its only endomorphism has trace $0$.

Here $\ker\rho=\{x\in H:\rho x=0\}$, using the kernel of a linear map from [[def-kernel-and-image-of-a-linear-map]]. The **support** of $\rho$ is the orthogonal complement of its kernel in the root convention:

$$\operatorname{supp}(\rho):=\{x\in H: \langle x,y\rangle=0\text{ for every }y\in\ker\rho\}.$$

For a subspace $S\subseteq H$, $\rho$ is **faithful on $S$** when $\operatorname{supp}(\rho)=S$ and the restriction $\rho|_S:S\to S$ is positive definite in the sense of [[def-non-negative-and-positive-operator]]. This restriction is an endomorphism: if $x\in S$ and $y\in\ker\rho$, self-adjointness gives $\langle\rho x,y\rangle=\langle x,\rho y\rangle=0$, so $\rho x\in(\ker\rho)^\perp=S$.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional vector space over $F$ and let $T:V\to V$ be
linear. Choose any ordered basis $\mathcal B$ of $V$ and define the **trace of
the endomorphism $T$** by

$$\operatorname{tr}(T):=\operatorname{tr}([T]_{\mathcal B}^{\mathcal B}).$$

This is independent of the chosen basis: matrices of the same endomorphism in
two ordered bases are similar, and similar matrices have equal trace. When
$V$ is the zero space, the empty basis gives trace $0$.

All complex inner products in this track use the root convention: they are
linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second
([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]). For vectors $x,y$ in the same
space, define the Dirac pairing by

$$\langle x|y\rangle_D:=\langle y,x\rangle_{\mathrm{root}}.$$

The ket $|x\rangle$ denotes the vector $x$. The bra $\langle x|$ denotes the
linear functional $z\mapsto\langle z,x\rangle_{\mathrm{root}}$.

For finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H,K$, vectors $y\in H$ and
$x\in K$, define the rank-one linear map

$$|x\rangle\langle y|:H\to K,\qquad z\mapsto\langle z,y\rangle_{H,\mathrm{root}}x.$$

Given ordered orthonormal bases of $H$ and $K$, its coordinate matrix is
$[x][y]^\dagger$, where $[x]$ and $[y]$ are the corresponding coordinate
columns and $M^\dagger:=\overline M^{\mathsf T}$ is the conjugate transpose.
The coordinate assertion is established in
[[thm-qc-dirac-notation-coordinate-identity]].

Let $H,K$ be finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces with ordered
orthonormal bases $E=(e_j)_{j<n}$ and $F=(f_i)_{i<m}$. Let $T:H\to K$ be
linear ([[def-linear-map]]), and write $T_{ij}$ for the $(i,j)$ entry of its
matrix in these bases.
Then, for every $z\in H$,

$$Tz=\sum_{j<n}\sum_{i<m}T_{ij}\langle z,e_j\rangle_{H,\mathrm{root}}f_i, \qquad T=\sum_{j<n}\sum_{i<m}T_{ij}|f_i\rangle\langle e_j|.$$

For $x\in K$ and $y\in H$, the rank-one map $|x\rangle\langle y|$ has
coordinate matrix $[x]_F[y]_E^\dagger$, where $M^\dagger=\overline M^{\mathsf T}$.
Its amplitude satisfies
$\langle x|T|y\rangle_D=\langle Ty,x\rangle_{K,\mathrm{root}}$.
All sums are empty when an index dimension is zero, and the identities include
those cases.

Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space and let $\Omega$ be a finite nonempty outcome set ([[def-dimension]], [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]). Its **endomorphisms** are its complex-linear maps $H\to H$ ([[def-vector-space-of-linear-maps]]); for an endomorphism $P$, $P^*$ denotes its adjoint, which exists uniquely in finite dimension ([[def-adjoint-of-a-linear-map-between-inner-product-spaces]], [[thm-adjoint-exists-and-is-unique-in-finite-dimension]]). A **finite projective measurement** on $H$ with outcomes $\Omega$ is a family $(P_a)_{a\in\Omega}$ of endomorphisms such that

$$P_a^*=P_a,\qquad P_a^2=P_a,\qquad P_aP_b=0\ (a\ne b),\qquad \sum_{a\in\Omega}P_a=I_H.$$

The products above are compositions, the sum is pointwise addition of endomorphisms, and $I_H$ is the identity map; these operations preserve linear maps ([[prop-linear-maps-form-a-vector-space]], [[lem-composition-and-identity-linear-maps]]). The projections $P_a=0$ are permitted. For a density operator $\rho$ on $H$ (nonnegative and trace one, [[def-qc-density-operator]]), the associated outcome weights are $p_\rho(a)=\operatorname{tr}(\rho P_a)$; their nonnegativity and normalization are proved in [[thm-qc-projective-measurement-outcome-law]].

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional vector space over $F$ and let $T:V\to V$ be
linear. Choose any ordered basis $\mathcal B$ of $V$ and define the **trace of
the endomorphism $T$** by

$$\operatorname{tr}(T):=\operatorname{tr}([T]_{\mathcal B}^{\mathcal B}).$$

This is independent of the chosen basis: matrices of the same endomorphism in
two ordered bases are similar, and similar matrices have equal trace. When
$V$ is the zero space, the empty basis gives trace $0$.

For every natural $n$, the map
$\operatorname{tr}:M_n(F)\to F$ is linear:

$$\operatorname{tr}(A+B)=\operatorname{tr}(A)+\operatorname{tr}(B),\qquad \operatorname{tr}(\lambda A)=\lambda\operatorname{tr}(A).$$

Let $G$ be a finite abelian group with character dual $\widehat G$ ([[def-qa-finite-abelian-character-dual]]). For a subgroup $H\le G$ ([[def-subgroup]]), define its character annihilator by
$$H^{\perp}:=\{\chi\in\widehat G:\chi(h)=1\text{ for every }h\in H\}.$$
For any subset $K\subseteq\widehat G$ (in particular, for any subgroup once $\widehat G$ has been proved to be a group), define
$$K^{\perp}:=\{g\in G:\chi(g)=1\text{ for every }\chi\in K\}.$$
The pairing is evaluation, and the same convention is used in both directions. `lem-qa-finite-abelian-annihilators-are-subgroups` proves that these sets are subgroups when the input is a subgroup.

Inputs are a hiding instance from [[def-qa-finite-abelian-hidden-subgroup-problem]], a fresh $b$-qubit group register and supplied exact circuits with declared access/costs, where $b$ is the group-code width in that definition:

- $P_G$ prepares the normalized uniform state $|G\rangle=N^{-1/2}\sum_{g\in G}|\operatorname{code}_G(g)\rangle$ on valid group labels and returns its workspace to the declared initial state.
- $O_F$ is the supplied coherent XOR oracle for the total extension $\widetilde F$ in [[def-qa-finite-abelian-hidden-subgroup-problem]], acting on the group register and a fresh $m$-qubit output register initialized to the all-zero word $0^m$.
- $Q_G$ is the supplied exact product QFT, with the fixed negative-character convention
$$Q_G|\operatorname{code}_G(g)\rangle=N^{-1/2}\sum_{\mathbf k}\overline{\chi_{\mathbf k}(g)}|\operatorname{code}_{\widehat G}(\mathbf k)\rangle$$
on the valid group subspace. It is supplied as a unitary on the full $b$-qubit register, so any extension from the valid-label subspace is part of the circuit input.

If $N=1$, return the unique trivial character without a query. Otherwise:

1. Prepare $|G\rangle$ with $P_G$.
2. Apply $O_F$ once to the group register and fresh output register.
3. Discard the output register by the declared partial-trace operation; do not measure it.
4. Apply $Q_G$ to the group register and measure the full $b$-qubit register in its ordered computational basis; the prescribed QFT action places the state in the valid character-code subspace.
5. Decode the measured valid character code as the tuple $\mathbf k$ and return $\chi_{\mathbf k}$.

This procedure assumes the preparation, oracle, and QFT circuits are supplied exactly. It makes no existence, uniformity, or efficiency claim for those circuits.

For an integer $d\ge 1$, the $d$-level register is the complex inner-product
space $Q_d=\mathbb C^d$ with the standard pairing
$\langle z,w\rangle_{\rm root}=\sum_{j<d}z_j\overline{w_j}$, linear in the
first argument as in [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]] and
[[prop-standard-coordinate-inner-products]]. Its **computational basis** is the
ordered standard basis $(e_0,\ldots,e_{d-1})$ of [[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]].
The register's alphabet is the ordered set $\{0,\ldots,d-1\}$.

For $n\ge0$, the $n$-qubit register is the ordered tensor product over
$\mathbb C$ of $n$ copies of $Q_2$. Here $\otimes_{\mathbb C}$ is the algebraic
module tensor product ([[def-tensor-product-of-modules-by-generators-and-relations]]),
with its complex-module structure and finite iterated/empty-product conventions
from [[thm-commutative-ring-module-structure-on-a-tensor-product]] and
[[cor-finite-iterated-tensor-products-represent-multilinear-maps]]. The tuple of
bit positions is ordered lexicographically, with the first wire as the most
significant position; the product-basis theorem below establishes the
corresponding elementary tensors as a basis. For $n=0$, the empty tensor
product is $\mathbb C$ with basis $\{1\}$. This one-dimensional trivial
register is distinct from the zero vector space $\mathbb C^0$. By definition a
register has positive dimension; a zero-dimensional space may still occur as a
factor in the more general tensor-space construction below.

For $n\ge0$ and a binary word $x=(x_0,\ldots,x_{n-1})\in\{0,1\}^n$, define its
**big-endian index**

$$\operatorname{enc}_n(x):=\sum_{k<n}x_k\,2^{\,n-1-k}.$$

Thus the first wire is the most significant bit. For $n=0$, the domain
$\{0,1\}^0$ consists only of the empty word $()$, and the empty sum gives
$\operatorname{enc}_0(())=0$. In an ordered $n$-qubit
computational basis, the word $x$ occupies the slot numbered
$\operatorname{enc}_n(x)$.

For every $d\ge1$, the ordered computational basis $(e_0,\ldots,e_{d-1})$ of
the register $Q_d$ from [[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]] is an
orthonormal basis for its declared inner product. Separately, the one-dimensional
zero-qubit register has the basis $\{1\}$ by definition.

An **ordered tensor register** consists of a finite ordered list of
finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H_0,\ldots,H_{n-1}$, each
equipped with a specified ordered orthonormal basis. Its space is
$H_0\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{n-1}$, with factors retained in the displayed
order. The product basis is ordered lexicographically by its tuple of factor
indices. The empty tensor product is $\mathbb C$ with basis $\{1\}$. A
zero-dimensional factor is allowed in this mathematical construction and makes
the tensor space zero; it is not a register under
[[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]].

The inner product is linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the
second, and on elementary tensors it is

$$\left\langle\bigotimes_{k<n}x_k,\bigotimes_{k<n}y_k\right\rangle_{\otimes}:=\prod_{k<n}\langle x_k,y_k\rangle_{{\rm root},k}.$$ 

For the empty tensor, the right side is the empty product $1$, giving the
standard inner product on $\mathbb C$.

For a permutation $\sigma$ of the $n$ factor positions, the **wire permutation**
$P_\sigma$ maps the product basis vector indexed by
$(i_0,\ldots,i_{n-1})$ to the product basis vector whose output factor order is
$(\sigma(0),\ldots,\sigma(n-1))$. It is extended linearly; for $n=0$ it is the
identity on $\mathbb C$. The extension is a linear map in the sense of
[[def-linear-map]].

Let $H_0,\ldots,H_{n-1}$ be a finite ordered list of finite-dimensional
complex inner-product spaces with specified ordered orthonormal bases of
sizes $d_0,\ldots,d_{n-1}$, allowing $d_k=0$. The elementary tensors of the
factor bases, ordered lexicographically, form an orthonormal basis of the
tensor register, and

$$\dim(H_0\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{n-1})=\prod_{k<n}d_k.$$

For the empty list the product is $1$ and the tensor space is $\mathbb C$; if
any $d_k=0$, the tensor space is zero and the product basis is empty.

An input group is given in explicit invariant-factor coordinates
$$G=\prod_{i=1}^r\mathbb Z/n_i\mathbb Z,\qquad 2\le n_1\mid n_2\mid\cdots\mid n_r,$$
with componentwise addition and $N:=|G|=\prod_i n_i$. The empty product has $G=\{0\}$ and $N=1$. No procedure for finding these coordinates from a black-box group is included. A character label is a tuple $\mathbf k=(k_1,\ldots,k_r)$ with $k_i\in\mathbb Z/n_i\mathbb Z$, representing
$$\chi_{\mathbf k}(\mathbf g):=\prod_{i=1}^r\exp(2\pi i k_i g_i/n_i).$$
The cyclic-character and product-character suppliers identify these labels with all of $\widehat G$.

The hiding input is a finite set $S$, an injective encoding $\eta:S\to\{0,1\}^m$, and a total function $F:G\to S$ for which there is an unknown subgroup $H\le G$ such that
$$F(\mathbf g)=F(\mathbf g')\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \mathbf g-\mathbf g'\in H.$$
This is the hiding promise. Put $b_i:=\lceil\log_2 n_i\rceil$ and $b:=\sum_i b_i$. Encode $g_i\in\mathbb Z/n_i\mathbb Z$ by the $b_i$-bit big-endian binary word of its least residue in $\{0,\ldots,n_i-1\}$, and encode $\mathbf g$ by concatenating these words in coordinate order; denote this injective code by $\operatorname{code}_G(\mathbf g)$. This uses the first-wire-most-significant-bit convention of [[def-qc-ordered-bitstring-encoding]]. Use the same coordinate widths and convention to encode character labels $\mathbf k$ as $\operatorname{code}_{\widehat G}(\mathbf k)$.

The hiding input also supplies a total Boolean function $\widetilde F:\{0,1\}^b\to\{0,1\}^m$ agreeing with $\eta\circ F$ on valid group codes; its values on invalid bit strings are part of the declared extension. The coherent XOR oracle acts by
$$O_{\widetilde F}|x,y\rangle=|x,y\oplus\widetilde F(x)\rangle$$
on all ordered input and target bit-string basis states. In particular, on valid codes it adds $\eta(F(\mathbf g))$ to the target. A named oracle call is charged as one query; a Boolean-circuit implementation is charged for its reversible gates. The model makes no claim that an arbitrary function has an efficient circuit.

The recovery algorithm outputs a finite list of character labels $\mathbf k^{(1)},\ldots,\mathbf k^{(M)}$. It denotes the constraint set
$$K:=\{\mathbf g\in G:\chi_{\mathbf k^{(j)}}(\mathbf g)=1\text{ for every }1\le j\le M\}=\bigcap_{j=1}^M\ker\chi_{\mathbf k^{(j)}},$$
where $\ker\chi:=\{\mathbf g:\chi(\mathbf g)=1\}$ and the empty intersection is defined to be $G$. Success means $K=H$. The output remains this implicit common-kernel presentation; converting it to subgroup generators is outside the definition.

derivations.claim: Fix a coset $g+H$ in the mixture of [F3] and write its transformed vector as $\psi_g=\sum_{\chi\in\widehat G}\alpha_{g,\chi}|\chi\rangle$. The input code ket is normalized by [F13], and the supplied circuit $Q_G$ is unitary by [F12], so $\|\psi_g\|=1$. For any vector $v$, [F8] gives $\langle\rho_gv,v\rangle_{\rm root}=|\langle v,\psi_g\rangle_{\rm root}|^2\ge0$ for $\rho_g=|\psi_g\rangle\langle\psi_g|$. In character coordinates, $\rho_g$ has diagonal entries $|\alpha_{g,\chi}|^2$, whose sum is $\|\psi_g\|^2=1$; [F7] gives $\operatorname{tr}(\rho_g)=1$. Thus [F6] makes $\rho_g$ a density operator.

The valid character-code basis is orthonormal by [F13], independently of the abstract matrix unitarity in [F5]. The exact action in [F12] places $\psi_g$ in its span, so every invalid $b$-bit outcome has probability zero. For a valid character $\chi$, its rank-one projector $P_\chi=|\chi\rangle\langle\chi|$ has a single diagonal $1$ at that code. The matrix of $\rho_g$ has entries $\alpha_{g,\mu}\overline{\alpha_{g,\nu}}$, so the projective-measurement weight [F9], computed by [F7]–[F8], is $\operatorname{tr}(\rho_gP_\chi)=|\alpha_{g,\chi}|^2$. By [F1], [F2], and the support definition [F11], this is $1/|H^\perp|$ when $\chi\in H^\perp$ and $0$ otherwise.

The probability in step 1.2 does not depend on the coset representative. The discarded-output state is the uniform mixture [F3], and trace linearity [F10] makes its measurement distribution the average of the same per-coset distribution. Hence the measured character is uniform on all of $H^\perp$ and has zero probability outside it.
By [F4], each supported outcome has probability $1/|H^\perp|=|H|/|G|$. In the boundary case $H=G$, the coset-transform formula [F1] gives the single trivial character with probability one.

citations.quote: For every finite abelian hidden-subgroup instance with hidden subgroup $H\le G$, one execution of the exact sample procedure returns a valid character code with probability one. Each $\chi\in H^\perp$ has probability $1/|H^\perp|=|H|/|G|$, every character outside $H^\perp$ has probability zero, and every invalid $b$-bit code has probability zero.

Let $G$ be a finite abelian group, and let $H\subsetneq K\le G$. Choose a character $\chi$ uniformly from $H^\perp$. Then
$$\mathbb P(\chi|_K\ne 1)\ge \frac12.$$
For every outcome with $\chi|_K\ne1$, the updated common kernel $K\cap\ker\chi$, where $\ker\chi=\{g\in G:\chi(g)=1\}$, contains $H$ and has index at least two in $K$.

Let $G$ be a finite abelian group with $N:=|G|\ge2$, let $H\le G$, and start with a current subgroup $K_0$ satisfying $H\le K_0\le G$. At each of $M$ fresh independent trials, if the current subgroup $K_{t-1}$ strictly contains $H$, draw a uniform $\chi_t\in H^\perp$ and replace $K_{t-1}$ by $K_t=K_{t-1}\cap\ker\chi_t$; after reaching $H$, leave the subgroup equal to $H$. Each cut reduces the current order by a factor of at least two. For $0<\delta<1$, put
$$s:=\left\lceil\log_2 N\right\rceil,\qquad M:=\left\lceil4s+16\ln(1/\delta)\right\rceil.$$
Then the failure event $K_M\ne H$ has probability at most $\delta$. If $H=K_0$, the failure probability is zero.

derivations.claim: If $|G|=1$, its only subgroup is $G$, and the algorithm outputs the empty constraint list denoting $G$. Thus the conclusion holds with probability one and zero queries.
Suppose $|G|\ge2$. Each measured character belongs to $H^\perp$ by [F1], so it is trivial on $H$. Hence every kernel in the output list contains $H$, and their intersection $K$ satisfies $H\le K$.

Starting with $K_0=G$, whenever $K_{t-1}>H$ the conditional cut probability and index reduction are those of [F2]. After $s=\lceil\log_2|G|\rceil$ cuts, the subgroup order is at most $|G|/2^s\le1$; since it contains the nonempty subgroup $H$, it must equal $H$.

The reconstruction procedure makes exactly $M$ independent samples. Therefore [F3] bounds the event that the final common kernel is not $H$ by $\delta$. Combining with $H\le K$ from step 1.2 gives success probability at least $1-\delta$.

Inputs are a hiding instance from [[def-qa-finite-abelian-hidden-subgroup-problem]], a fresh $b$-qubit group register and supplied exact circuits with declared access/costs, where $b$ is the group-code width in that definition:

$$Q_G|\operatorname{code}_G(g)\rangle=N^{-1/2}\sum_{\mathbf k}\overline{\chi_{\mathbf k}(g)}|\operatorname{code}_{\widehat G}(\mathbf k)\rangle$$
on the valid group subspace. It is supplied as a unitary on the full $b$-qubit register, so any extension from the valid-label subspace is part of the circuit input.

5. Decode the measured valid character code as the tuple $\mathbf k$ and return $\chi_{\mathbf k}$.

An input group is given in explicit invariant-factor coordinates

derivations.claim: For $N\ge2$, the reconstruction algorithm executes exactly $M$ independent sample procedures by [F1]. Under the Statement's no-access hypothesis for $P_G$ and $Q_G$, each sample's explicit hiding-oracle call is its only access to that oracle, so the query coordinate is exactly $M$. $$R_{\mathbf n}(\theta):=\exp\!\left(-\frac{i\theta}{2}\mathbf n\cdot\boldsymbol{\sigma}\right),\qquad R_z(\theta):=R_{(0,0,1)}(\theta).$$

For a family $(C_n)$ with a specified full-list generator $G$, let $t_G(n)$ be the worst-case number of Turing-machine transitions used by $G$ on unary input $1^n$. For a total acceptance predicate $A_n(x,z)$, let $t_A(n)$ and $s_A(n)$ be its worst-case deterministic transition count and tape-space use over all valid length-$n$ inputs and measured outputs, using a fixed effective encoding of the pair $(x,z)$. Any effective input description, classical preprocessing, or threshold computation has its own bit length and time/space bounds; these costs are not included in $t_G$ or $t_A$ unless the same machine performs them. The machine conventions are those of [[def-deterministic-one-tape-turing-machine]], [[def-partial-function-computed-by-a-machine]], and [[def-worst-case-time-and-space-complexity]].

If the access model explicitly supplies a named oracle gate $\mathcal O$, let $q_{\mathcal O}(C)$ be the number of calls to it. With several named oracles, record a separate query coordinate for each. Ordinary finite-basis gates, oracle calls, circuit-description length, generator time, and classical bit costs remain separate; no oracle, controlled-oracle, inverse-oracle, or data-loading operation is assigned zero cost unless its interface explicitly says so.

For an approximate task with declared rational tolerance $0<\epsilon<1$, let $\ell(\epsilon)$ be the bit length of that exact binary-rational encoding. Exact finite-gate computations have no precision field. The **cost record** consists of all applicable coordinates
$$\bigl(L(C_n),g(C_n),d(C_n),w(C_n),a_{\rm clean}(C_n),a_{\rm dirty}(C_n),t_G(n),t_A(n),s_A(n),q_{\mathcal O}(C_n),\epsilon,\ell(\epsilon)\bigr).$$
An inapplicable coordinate is marked not applicable, not silently charged as zero. This definition records the resource model; separate theorems establish polynomial bounds.
